91ae548d2cb1abf2: Advisers for COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago, center, talk after a Colombia delegate's request to speak was overlooked at the U.N. summit in 2025. Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty ImagesNearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem. It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat. In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher. Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises. There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader. As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks. As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change: 1. Say we can’t afford it “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target. Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030. In reality, affordability is really about priorities. For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy. Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels. The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it. 2. Promise to fix it later Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided. This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “stabilization wedge” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy. Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground. Congressional Budget Office Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue. Scientists, including one of the original authors, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP. Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks. 3. Water down the promise Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding. At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement. However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most. U.S. Climate Envoy John Kerry and other delegates huddle for final negotiating at the closing sessions of COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021. Kiara Worth/UNFCCC, CC BY-NC-SA The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out. 4. Make promises, then fail to deliver Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding. In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade. Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting, with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid. The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster. Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage. Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork. 5. Make decisions without everyone at the table Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel. At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach. In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out. After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened. What to watch for at COP31 At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice. Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions, where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers. My team will be tracking what happens, whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.” Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article. ee0305ab71b3feaa: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty ImagesData centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally. Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations. These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away. The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Politics as usual As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president. It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day. As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. 4b382a44aa6e09e6: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.
The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.
Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.
Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).
The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.
A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.
Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.
It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

05bd9f0351a0c3a2: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

ce8b9f01db91226b: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders.

The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation.
Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access.

Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns.

The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers.

Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity.

There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised.

It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion.

Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed.

Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected.

Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer.
The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

d8283c68ecae5ae4: "AI delusion" remains loosely defined, but most of us know it when we see it: exaggerated faith in the technology's power, applicability, or nature, coupled with a refusal to acknowledge its limitations.

It's bad in the individual, as when an elderly relative emails you a hallucination-laden ChatGPT summary. It's worse in management, when your boss insists that AI slop is genius marketing content at a bargain rate. It is terrifying in tech CEOs. It is not, thankfully, compulsory.

Consider three recent examples of technology leadership in the age of AI. One would be Pythonesque were the disconnect with engineers and the public not so profound. Another risks becoming a business-school case study in how to demolish customer trust. The third offers something less fashionable: robust pragmatism. Saving the best till last, y'all.

Case 1: we present for your consideration Sam Altman of OpenAI, one of the few actually at the controls of the singularity machine. It seems churlish to pluck just one luscious fruit out of that cornucopia of choices, yet we must. Sam Altman thinks it is a sin against the natural order that so much RAM is idling in machines owned by individuals, organizations, and anywhere that isn't Big AI. It's oh so inefficient. How convenient that the efficient allocation of scarce resources should favor the business he runs. Free market schmarket.
Altman has since said his remarks were taken out of context and that he wants consumers to have as much memory as they like. The efficiency argument still reveals whose priorities come first.

This is the best kind of delusion, one with an undeniable truth at its core – memory does indeed get used far more intensively in AI model makers and inference servers than in your laptop. For a business selling the future, treating privately owned hardware as an inefficient allocation of resources has a distinctly Soviet flavor, and the American right has vowed to stamp out socialist extremism. Get on with it, chaps, you've only got two years left. That Altman can't see this is the best bit of the misconception.

There are two potential root causes of this Marxist-Leninist-Altmanism. One is that he's mathed the math and worked out that the only way OpenAI can hit the numbers is if it gets every last byte in the world, hot off the fab. The other is that you can't run on-prem on an 8 GB state-mandated Chromebook, and on-prem is otherwise going to twist his melon until it falls off.

Case 2: Andy Yen, CEO of Proton, the company behind Proton Mail and Proton VPN. You, me, and the household cat know ProtonMail as the secondary email that's worth paying for. You want the best recovery backup email for Gmail, you want it as an accessible end-to-end encrypted email service. You want it because it is all about stable spotless security, all about the end users, all about being there when you absolutely need it. It is safe to recommend, and you do.

Or rather that's what you thought about ProtonMail et al until the same day you learned about Andy Yen's alleged behavior. Leaked comms reported by 404 Media allege Yen saw Proton as a company that must make its numbers come what may, and one path to do that was to AI-code at maximum velocity.

Engineers who wanted to test the results for security were losers – fax machine operators in the internet age – and he didn't want them, or so the report claimed. No more engineers, just product managers in a Claude terminal. He allegedly imparted this vision through aggression, belittling employees in front of their peers, and swinging his big ol' reinterview job chopper.

More generally, running a toxic workplace should lead to instant dismissal and loss of license to be in charge of anything more sentient than a sausage machine. That AI is involved is not AI's fault. Misunderstanding the brand and the customer base so, so badly – that's the delusion.
ProtonMail has a unique niche, an important part of the whole. People depend on it because privacy and security are the proposition.

Putting velocity of coding above that is arrant stupidity. Nobody cares. Unless new features and products increase security, they'll only matter outside the niche, where one might argue that Proton products cannot compete. Not knowing that, has the potential to destroy a brand overnight. Yen wouldn't be the first CEO to cause a company some trouble by revealing what they really think, but this one matters. Things are being rowed back – no more reinterviewing to prove allegiance to AI at all costs, and an employee has said it's not quite as bad as all that.

Case 3: Linus Torvalds. He reports that AI-based kernel code has not saturated the production pipeline, is useful when treated properly, and the kernel cadence is expanding following a stabilization period. The high-pressure AI patch spigot turned on; the appropriate plumbing was created to regulate and filter; and he is much happier now.

It's a nuanced story, and nuance is so often a dirty word in the industry. Torvalds' happiness is not a guarantee that everything in the garden is in fact lovely, but the Linus vibe is as good as any – and it's better than most predictive metrics. He is hitting his numbers, which are the quality of the code and the speed at which changes match what users need in a changing world. The numbers do not involve margins, profits, shareholder value, or driving massive investment before the gig's up.

Put another way, Torvalds has managed the arrival of AI to probably the most important codebase ever, and he has done it with, not in spite of, the most diverse and independently minded dev team that ever came through the merge window, and it's barely news. If only they gave Oscars for this sort of thing.

There is no better advert for sanity, nor for FOSS's unique and infinitely valuable ability to remain responsive to market forces without market dependency. Freedom cures delusion. Even AI delusion. It's a helluva drug. ®
1534ef685e30d232: Attackers stole central university login passwords belonging to everyone registered with the Technical University of Munich's myTUM portal, including an admin whose credentials were then used to attack a second system.
TUM restored access to its TUMonline campus management system on Monday morning, allowing users to change their passwords.

The university disclosed the attack on November 6. The initial attack targeted the myTUM portal, which serves students and faculty members, providing centralized online access to services and documents.
TUM said the attackers used the admin's credentials to launch a follow-on attack on TUMonline, its central campus management system, which forced the IT team to take it offline.
The university has not disclosed how the attackers initially gained access or how the stolen passwords were stored. It did not immediately answer questions about the number of affected users.
It also did not specify whether this sysadmin had multi-factor authentication (MFA) switched on, but it confirmed that "user accounts with MFA were protected from this attack."

Attackers may also have accessed names, home addresses, and dates of birth. Potentially exposed employee records included work addresses and phone numbers, while student records included ID numbers, degree programs, and completed semesters.

"The attackers' access within TUMonline was largely logged," said Dr Alexander Braun, CIO at TUM, in the disclosure. "After analyzing these logs, we currently assume that no other data from TUMonline was compromised, such as grades or college applications. We are continuing to investigate this."

TUM is directing users to reset their passwords through Microsoft 365 where possible. Those without MFA already configured must instead use a German electronic ID or request a reset email while connected to the campus network.
The university also warned users to watch for phishing and fraud, and to change any passwords reused elsewhere.

TUM ranks first in Germany and 25th worldwide in the QS university rankings. The STEM-focused institution reports 51,954 students across its German campuses and TUM Asia in Singapore, plus 12,850 employees. ®

ab138347ee884e3e: NEW YORK, Nov 9 — Chips made by US chip titan Nvidia push the boundaries of artificial intelligence, but its leader Jensen Huang is in the spotlight over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Unknown to the public just four years ago, the 63-year-old is a powerful entrepreneur, drawing stadium crowds as he presents cutting-edge components essential to the development of AI tools like ChatGPT.
Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funnelling information to Beijing.
Nvidia’s board said yesterday it had opened a probe into the CEO and co-founder, who acknowledged having been unfaithful to his wife and said he was “deeply sorry.”

Big tech’s insatiable appetite for chips designed by Nvidia, known as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), has catapulted the California chipmaker to a market valuation of US$4.5 trillion (RM18.2 trillion), among the world’s largest.

Its meteoric rise has made Huang one of the world’s richest people — worth around US$160 billion, according to Forbes — thanks to the roughly four per cent stake he holds in the company he founded three decades ago with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner.
He has become a close informal adviser on AI to Donald Trump, travelling with the US president on Air Force One on a trip to Beijing earlier this year.
That is an area of concern to US officials who believe he has been involved with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, who is linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, according to the New York Times.
Despite their shared surname, the pair are not related.
Early life
Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang — originally named Jen-Hsun — embodies the American success story.
At nine years old, he was sent away with his brother to boarding school in small-town Kentucky.
His uncle recommended the school to his Taiwanese parents believing it to be a prestigious institution, though it was actually a school for troubled youth.

Too young to be a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. With his poor English, he was bullied and forced to clean toilets — a two-year ordeal that transformed him.
“We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough,” he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.
But “the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there,” Huang said.
Brought home by his parents who had by then settled in the north-western US state of Oregon, he graduated from university at just 20 and joined AMD, then LSI Logic, to design chips — his passion.

But he wanted to go further and founded Nvidia in 1993 to “solve problems that normal computers can’t,” using semiconductors powerful enough to handle 3D graphics, he said during an interview on the “No Priors” podcast.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang waves after a welcome ceremony for US President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing May 14, 2026. Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade. — AFP pic
‘As fast as we can’
Nvidia created the first GPU in 1999, riding the intersection of video games, data centres, cloud computing and now generative AI.
Always dressed in a black T-shirt and leather jacket, Huang sports a Nvidia logo tattoo and has a taste for sports cars.
One former high-ranking Nvidia employee described him to AFP as “the most driven person” he’d ever met.
He has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade.
“That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention,” but “it’s not grounded on facts,” he told CBS News in September.
“We should go as fast as we can” on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.
Street food
On visits to his native Taiwan, Huang is treated like a megastar, with fans crowding him for autographs and selfies as journalists follow him to the barber shop and his favourite night market.
“He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm,” noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute.

“A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan,” he said, calling Huang “unusually friendly.”
Over the years, Nvidia has taken care to project a drama-free image of Huang.

But the former employee painted a more nuanced picture, describing a “very paradoxical” individual fiercely protective of his employees but also capable, within Nvidia’s executive circle, of “ripping people to shreds” over major mistakes or poor choices. — AFP

0eb379a3880421ea: A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it.

AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on.

The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience.

Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response.
"Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before.
"It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said.

The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music submitted, although he still listens to every track to make sure nobody is trying to pass off Bohemian Rhapsody as their own work.
Among the early offerings are what Chaffin describes as a developing genre of slightly rude protest songs about HR departments, along with an operatic epic about a blocked toilet.
"Some of which are hilarious," he said of the HR songs. As for the toilet opera, it "runs through my head about once a day, whether I like it or not."

Chaffin believes the sheer volume of music uploaded to streaming platforms means plenty of perfectly decent tracks never find an audience, whether a person or a machine made them. He hopes AI Slop FM will give some of those overlooked creations a chance to be heard.
"You don't have to have published your creations to upload. Just to own the rights," he explained.
Tracks that don't make the Slop 40 could still get another outing, with plans for genre-specific stations offering unsuccessful submissions a second chance.
The bigger question is what happens when listeners start rating AI-generated music more highly than the human competition, but Chaffin isn't particularly worried about that.
"If the machines win then their creators clearly deserve to be heard, deserve an audience. If the musicians win, then that's reassuring for them."

He also wants to see how the station's eventual top five or top ten compares with the official music charts, although with submissions having only recently opened, there are no results to pore over just yet.
"Everyone has an opinion on music before a note has been heard, by the genre, the label, the name or the cover art," Chaffin said. "We strip all that away, tracks are judged purely on the music."

Whether listeners ultimately prefer human musicians or their algorithmically assisted rivals remains to be seen. Either way, somewhere in Carmarthenshire, an opera about a blocked toilet is proving rather difficult to flush from its listener's memory. ®

111b66d97ab01eca: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.

Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.

But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.

Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.

The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.

In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.

But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.

The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.

Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.

The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.

Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.

Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.
The need has never been more apparent.
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.
daed6fa86fdbaa3d: DUNGUN, Nov 9 — A total of 69 participants in the Projek Berkelompok Kelapa Kampung Dendang, here, claim that their income has been affected since the beginning of this year due to an influx of imported coconuts in the market from Indonesia since the start of the year.

Project head Mohamed Zakaria Awang, 66, said that most wholesalers and traders of coconuts and coconut milk here prefer to source imported coconuts from Indonesia because they are cheaper compared to local ones.
He said that the situation caused a decrease in demand for the Matang variety of coconuts produced by the project participants, which in turn affected their sales and income.
Some 5,000 coconut trees across 20 hectares cultivated by participants of the Kampung Dendang Coconut Group Farming Project in Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
Overall, the participants of the group project planted 5,000 coconut trees over an area of 20 hectares in 2009 and started yielding results in 2012.

“Every month, the growers can harvest about 500 coconuts to sell to wholesalers and coconut milk traders as our source of income,” he said when met at the Projek Berkelompok Kelapa Kampung Dendang site here today.

Mohamed Zakaria said that currently, the coconuts produced by the project’s participants are being purchased by the Federal Agricultural Marketing Authority (Fama) at a price of RM1.10 each to help market the growers’ produce following the influx of imported coconuts in the market, compared to RM2.50 each which were sold to wholesalers and traders previously.
Unsold coconuts pile up following an influx of supply from Indonesia since early this year, affecting their income, during a site visit in Kampung Dendang, Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
“All this time, coconut growers were able to earn more than RM2,000 a month, but that amount has dropped to around RM500 a month currently due to the drop in coconut prices.
“Meanwhile, imported coconuts from Indonesia are sold at only 80 sen each in the market, putting pressure on the prices of local coconuts,” he said.

Another project participant, Zahari Abdullah, 61, said that some participants are no longer interested in continuing the group project due to the decline in coconut prices since the start of this year.
He said that the situation caused some of the participants’ coconut plantations to no longer be properly managed, even though the trees were still producing yields.
Unsold coconuts pile up following an influx of supply from Indonesia since early this year, affecting their income, during a site visit in Kampung Dendang, Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
“If this situation continues, we are worried that more participants will decide to leave this project because the sales results can no longer provide returns like before,” he said.
Meanwhile, Terengganu Fama director Muhamad Fadlee Hassan said that his team had purchased coconuts from the group participants from April 29 to November 3.
“The coconuts that are purchased will be marketed to local wholesalers and Fama retail outlets around the Kuala Terengganu district,” he added. — Bernama
af88f9028914f21b: Rising memory prices are pushing more customers toward refurbished tech, suppliers say, with warranties of up to three years helping to make secondhand kit a less daunting purchase.
Memory costs have more than quadrupled this year as manufacturers prioritize more lucrative high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for servers powering AI datacenters.

Many enterprises are keeping equipment longer in an uncertain economy. Ben Caddy, senior analyst at Omdia, said suppliers were linking refresh discussions with opportunities to recover value from customers' aging kit.

By 2030, he predicted, 35 percent of "all the hardware sold for the channel will be taken back by partners," driven "by the sheer economic logic of taking equipment back, recovering value, and embracing more circular IT lifecycles."

This is already helping some customers "unlock some capital to put towards those [relatively] small refresh plans," he said while hosting a panel on circular IT at last month's Canalys Forums in Barcelona.
Refurbished smartphones are growing in popularity, but persuading customers to trade in their old devices remains a constraint on supply.
The same applies to PCs and other equipment, said Jon Sansom, MD at GreenSafe IT. "Availability is a challenge," he said.

Marcel Joosten, group director of marketing and digital commerce at tech lifecycle specialist XTENTEC, said the company now offers trade-ins when customers buy new kit. "We're actually financing the residual value" at the end of year two, three, or four, when customers return the equipment, he told the audience.

XTENTEC collects, refurbishes, rents, and resells equipment, and has an agreement with HP to renovate aging products, with a two or even three-year warranty available as "just an SKU on the list from HP."
Joosten said equivalent support, including HP Care Pack services, helped make refurbished equipment more attractive to buyers.
Customers want to cut their carbon footprint, and many public and private sector tenders require it. But the "most important thing" for many is trust, said Patrick Molberg, CEO of Advania Finance.

"The customers have to trust the refurbished equipment and have to trust the process. And I think one of the things that we have to be better at as a whole is that we kind of need to have a standard methodology regarding verification."

Work on verification standards with vendors including HP, Lenovo, and Dell is ongoing, Molberg said. He also argued that lifecycle services should be built into purchasing decisions rather than added three or four years later.

Joosten argued that listed US tech companies' focus on quarterly sales and market share can work against refurbishment. "That needs to change," he said. "I think there should be a market share figure for circularity." ®

ff24ba8d59b95a21: Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software.

This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal.
Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time.
In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption.

"We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register, he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?"

What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work.
"Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote.
The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked.
"In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register.
Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake.

"To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem.
The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point.
The day before the holiday, a customer volunteered their machine.

This customer was located a few hours away by road, so an engineer got the job of visiting on the morning of the holiday to pick up the stricken machine, give the customer a shiny new system and configure it to their specifications.
Said engineer did the job, which took so long he was invited to stay for the holiday meal, then returned to HQ with the broken box.
The next day, Oriel and his colleagues got to work and found a fix, then created a version of the accounting application that wouldn't break any more PCs.

Oriel was, of course, summoned into a meeting with senior execs to explain the situation and watched as they decided the best course of action was to pull buggy CDs from stores – which meant trashing CDs and packaging valued at $1 million.
Have you made a mistake that broke customers' kit, or cost millions? If so, don't make the mistake of not sharing your story with The Register and click here to email the column. ®
c35a133ff9697d5c: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang. Used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.
The business of knowing more about us

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
Inclusion at what cost?

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.
Nigeria’s data protection challenge

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.
Innovation must not come at the expense of control

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.
Written by Nshua Cali-Dibang

a0f61c6c0cf5cc52: From Khin Nadarajah and Sri Nadarajah
The 2027 budget brings fresh momentum to Malaysia’s preparations for longer lives.

Its wider investment commitments, including RM25 billion from government-linked investment companies, provide a timely setting to consider how capital, housing and care can work together for older Malaysians.

The opportunity is to translate that momentum into responsible investment in care, housing, healthcare, technology and services that families can depend on. The task is to turn that momentum into services that families can depend on.

The scale is clear. Asean’s population aged 60 and over stood at 74.4 million in 2020 and is projected to reach 127 million by 2035. The speed matters, too. France had 115 years to make the transition to an aged society. Malaysia will have about 27 years.

The statistics department's preliminary estimates for 2026 put the population aged 60 and above at 4.2 million, or 12.3% of the total. These figures make healthy ageing an immediate infrastructure and investment priority.

The recent call by the finance ministry to invest responsibly in the longevity economy remains an important starting point. As proposals take shape, it helps to keep their purpose in view: preserving independence, supporting changing needs and creating lasting value for both families and investors.
Care becomes investable when we can show that the service works for people as well as the numbers work for capital.
We should begin with the person rather than the building.

The National Health and Morbidity Survey 2025 found that 60% of older Malaysians were pre-frail, representing about 2.4 million people. Another 10.7% were already frail. This strengthens the case for earlier support, before greater dependency develops.

Most people hope to remain independent and connected to familiar surroundings for as long as they can. Their needs may then change gradually, or suddenly after an illness or a fall. A useful care system must offer choices between living at home with support and receiving more intensive help. Day services, rehabilitation, home nursing, assisted living and residential care each have a place.

The surroundings matter, too. A home that worked well at 45 may be harder to manage at 75. Stairs, maintenance, transport and access to healthcare can become obstacles. This does not necessarily mean someone needs residential care. It may mean the environment needs to adapt so that independence can continue.

The property sector, therefore, has a role beyond supplying more retirement units. Adaptable homes, accessible public spaces, walkable neighbourhoods and connections to health and community services can help people remain active and involved. Independence should be understood through the life a person can lead, as well as where they live.
This has consequences for development. A well-designed building matters, alongside its continuing usefulness as residents’ needs change.

Early collaboration with the care operator can help align design, skilled staffing and the support families may need over time. Clear information about services and costs helps families plan with greater confidence.
For families, the real test is simple: will this place still be right for someone they love when that person needs more help?

These considerations also strengthen the investment case. Local demand, sustainable pricing, staffing, governance and long-term maintenance deserve attention together. An adaptable, operationally viable development can better serve residents and sustain investor confidence.
The reduction in service tax on elderly care, together with the exemption announced in the 2027 budget, offers welcome relief for families.

They also provide a useful occasion to consider affordability across the full range of needs, from accommodation and daily living to more intensive care. Middle-income families and lower-income households should remain part of that planning. Affordability cannot be added as an afterthought.

Developers, care providers, insurers, employers and policymakers each have a role in exploring practical ways for people to pay for support across different stages of needs. Different households will need different arrangements. Community services, rental options and supported access can complement ownership models, where local evidence and sustainable funding support them.

The announced allocation of more than RM40 million to train 8,000 people in elderly care reinforces the importance of the workforce. Training, supervision and staff retention deserve the same early attention as land and buildings. Investing in people helps turn a well-designed setting into dependable and trustworthy care.
The proposed Senior Citizens Bill is a further reminder of the value of clear responsibility and accountability.
Safeguarding, transparent fees, accessible complaints procedures and standards that can be monitored help families, operators and investors build confidence together.

The same care should guide how progress is measured. Alongside beds built and units sold, attention should go to residents’ social connections, consistent care, timely support and staff development. These outcomes help show whether investment is adding value to everyday life.

One of us, Sri Nadarajah, was born in Malaysia and spent much of his working life developing businesses abroad. That experience taught him to respect both ambition and execution. A promising idea must survive contact with the practical details: land, finance, operations, people and accountability.
Malaysia does not need to choose between commercial discipline and doing good. The strongest care investments will require both.
The budget provides momentum; thoughtful partnerships can carry it forward. Institutional capital has a role alongside government, communities and responsible private operators.

With local evidence, adaptable design and clear delivery responsibilities, Malaysia can build homes and services that remain dependable as lives change. That is how longevity becomes part of the country’s working social infrastructure.
Khin Nadarajah and Sri Nadarajah are the founders of Venus Healthcare, a specialist care provider.
